sources.title: Wifredo Lam (Q465342), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-31): label 'Wifredo Lam', description 'Cuban artist (1902-1982)', born 1902-12-08, died 1982-09-11, Korean label present, image 'Wilfredo Lam.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Wifredo Lam', read in full (about 5,000 characters). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: a Cuban painter known for his synthesis of Modernist aesthetics and Afro-Cuban imagery; study in Havana and Madrid, flight from Barcelona to Paris in 1938 with a letter to Picasso, membership of the Surrealist movement after meeting Breton, return to Cuba in 1941 where he developed his signature style, and The Jungle (1943) with its hybrid human, animal and plant figures among sugarcane and banana leaves. Tertiary reference article; short.

Tate Modern, 'Who is Wifredo Lam?' (exhibition guide for The EY Exhibition: Wifredo Lam, 2016-17), read in the sections on his career, themes, influences and quotations: scholarship in Madrid and study of the Prado, the move to Paris in 1938 and Picasso's introductions, his own remark that surrealism gave him an opening but he had not painted in a surrealist manner, and the return to Havana in 1941. Museum exhibition text written to promote the show, so it is admiring in tone.

Lowery Stokes Sims, 'Lam, Wifredo', Encyclopedia of African-American Culture and History (2005, via Encyclopedia.com), read in full (about 1,000 words): study in Havana and Spain, the Paris and Marseilles years with the Surrealists, the first masterpieces made in Cuba from 1942 to 1945 including The Jungle, the later studio in Italy, his role as mentor and associate to the CoBrA, Phases and Situationist generation, and the author's closing judgement of his legacy. Scholarly reference entry by the author of a monograph on Lam; it makes the strong claim that he was 'the first artist of color to make an impact on the international art scene', which is not repeated here as fact.

'Wifredo Lam', Cuban Painters biography page (cubanet.org), read in full (about 1,000 words): year-by-year outline of his schooling, Spain until 1938, the Paris circle, Marseilles activities (the Tarot de Marseille, collective drawings, six drawings for Breton's Fata Morgana), the 1941 meeting with Aime Cesaire, the effect of the Cuban landscape and Afro-Cuban heritage on his work, the 1946 Haiti visit, the move to graphics and ceramics, and the exhibition record. Unsigned encyclopedic summary of uncertain authorship; it dates his first Paris solo show to 1929 where other sources give 1939, so it is used only for the outline and not for dates.

Centre Pompidou, press kit for the exhibition 'Wifredo Lam' (30 September 2015 - 15 February 2016), read in full (about 2,500 words, PDF): five chronological sections (Spain, Paris and Marseille, Cuba and the Americas, Paris-Caracas-Havana-Albisola-Zurich, and the later years), his collaborations with painters, poets and intellectuals, the role of Lydia Cabrera, Fernando Ortiz and Alejo Carpentier in his search for 'Cubanness', and his contact with the CoBrA artists. Exhibition text by the museum; the political passages are not used for any score.

Ben Davis, 'How Wifredo Lam Made Surrealism More Surreal Than the Surrealists', Artnet News (17 February 2026), read in full: a critic's essay on the MoMA exhibition 'When I Don't Sleep, I Dream' that questions both the 'Cuba's Picasso' reading and the purely 'Afro-Cuban' reading, notes that Lam was a sympathetic observer rather than a practitioner of Santeria, quotes his statements to Max-Pol Fouchet, describes the Marseilles collective games, and records that The Jungle was painted on paper for lack of canvas. Independent critical voice; the opinion is the writer's and the interview quotations are relayed second-hand.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_lam_eb, src_lam_tate, src_lam_sims, src_lam_pomp, src_lam_artnet | 1941-1945 | institutional + scholarly + critical] Britannica says that in Cuba he developed a signature style blending Cubism and Surrealism, African and Afro-Cuban art and Cuba's colours and vegetation, with The Jungle's hybrid human, animal and plant figures; Sims lists the recurring motifs he kept varying (bamboo, tobacco leaves, the horse-headed woman). The critic Davis complicates the story, arguing that the Marseilles collective games shaped the figures as much as Picasso did and that neither the 'applied Cubism' nor the purely 'Afro-Cuban' reading fits, which supports an original synthesis without calling it single-sourced invention. Most of the praise comes from museums and a monograph author, with one critic as the only outside check. cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_lam_eb, src_lam_cuba, src_lam_pomp, src_lam_sims | 1923-1960s | reference + institutional] He combined European modernist styles with African and Afro-Cuban sources and moved among the media of painting, drawing, book illustration (six drawings for Breton's Fata Morgana, a Spanish edition of Cesaire's poem), a Surrealist card deck, and from the late 1950s graphics and ceramics, the latter including terracotta work prompted by the CoBrA artists. The range is across styles and media within the visual arts and its literary circle rather than across separate professions, so it is held at a moderate level.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_lam_tate, src_lam_artnet, src_lam_sims | 1938-1976 | institutional + critical, with self-report relayed] Tate quotes his remark that surrealism gave him an opening but he had not painted in a surrealist manner; Davis quotes him saying he does not use symbolism and invents from a poetic stimulus, and notes he was a sympathetic observer rather than a practitioner of Santeria; Sims reports his conviction that his work was an instrument of liberation. These are his own statements relayed second-hand, and the independent evidence for his working method is the critic's reading, so the row stays modest.

collaboration.rationale: [src_lam_cuba, src_lam_artnet, src_lam_pomp, src_lam_sims | 1940-1960s | reference + critical + institutional] At Marseilles in 1940-41 he took part in the Surrealists' group activities, the Tarot de Marseille and the collective drawings, and illustrated Breton's poem; he lent his art to a Spanish edition of Cesaire's poem; the Centre Pompidou describes his collaborations with many painters, poets and intellectuals, and Sims calls him a mentor as well as associate of the CoBrA, Phases and Situationist generation. The documented behaviour is shared creative work and mentoring in artistic circles; it says little about how he worked with individuals day to day.

adaptability.rationale: [src_lam_eb, src_lam_pomp, src_lam_artnet, src_lam_sims | 1923-1952 | reference + institutional + critical] He worked in Havana, Madrid, Paris, Marseilles, then again in Cuba, Haiti, New York and Italy, shifting between academic, Cubist, Surrealist and later more schematic idioms; the critic notes The Jungle was painted on a large sheet of paper because he had no canvas when he got to Cuba. The movements were driven by war and exile, so the evidence shows how he kept producing under changing conditions rather than a preference for change, and no inner state is inferred.
